site.title: Cults, Panics and Mass Hysteria by Country
site.description: Country-by-country guides to cults, moral panics, mass hysteria, social scares, and collective belief episodes.

pages.title: When Fear Became Fact in Afghanistan
pages.summary: Afghanistan’s history contains no well-documented equivalent of the European witch craze or a single famous home-grown “cult panic”.

pages.title: Farkhunda
pages.summary: A false claim of Quran burning became fatal within minutes, revealing how sacred outrage, crowd action and failed policing can combine.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear Became Fact in Afghanistan.

pages.title: School Scares
pages.summary: Repeated school illnesses blurred the line between genuine attack fears, contagious distress and official claims made before evidence was complete.

pages.title: Crisis of Trust
pages.summary: Decades of conflict made hidden plots seem plausible, allowing rumours about schools, health campaigns and foreign interference to spread quickly.

pages.title: When Fear and Belief Shook Albania
pages.summary: Albania’s clearest episode of contagious collective belief was not a witch craze or an outbreak of unexplained illness. It was the nationwide investment fever that preceded the collapse of fraudulent financial schemes in 1996–97.

pages.title: Pyramid Crisis
pages.summary: Fraudulent investment schemes spread through trust and imitation before their collapse helped trigger armed disorder in 1997.

pages.title: Witch Beliefs
pages.summary: Folklore and one disputed killing reveal harmful supernatural accusations without proving that Albania experienced an organised witch hunt.

pages.title: Religion Ban
pages.summary: The communist state tried to eliminate religion through closures, propaganda and punishment while demanding unquestioning faith in the party.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Belief Shook Albania.

pages.title: When Fear Became a Public Threat in Algeria
pages.summary: Algeria’s history offers no well-documented equivalent of the Salem witch trials or a famous dancing plague. Its most revealing episodes of collective fear instead involve rumours of hidden enemies, accusations of religious subversion, supernatural harm, online threats and sudden crowd violence.

pages.title: Ahmadiyya
pages.summary: Hundreds of Ahmadis faced investigation or prosecution after officials recast peaceful minority worship as a foreign-backed threat.

pages.title: Colonial Fear
pages.summary: French officials treated religious networks as possible channels of rebellion, turning uncertainty into surveillance and recurring conspiracy fears.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear Became a Public Threat in Algeria.

pages.title: Karakaria
pages.summary: Unusual dress and unfamiliar Sufi teachings became evidence of hidden danger despite limited proof of coercion or foreign control.

pages.title: How Witch Fear Took Hold in Andorra
pages.summary: Andorra’s clearest documented episode of contagious fear is not a modern “cult panic” or outbreak of mass psychogenic illness, but a long series of witchcraft prosecutions between the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries. Surviving court records describe roughly 180 women who were denounced or investigated, with at least 15 known executions.

pages.title: Courts and Power
pages.summary: Local secular judges, not the Spanish Inquisition, ordered the known executions and gave village rumours legal force.

pages.title: Trial Timeline
pages.summary: Court records trace two centuries of accusations, prosecutions and at least 15 known executions across Andorra.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on How Witch Fear Took Hold in Andorra.

pages.title: Fear Spreads
pages.summary: Quarrels, illness, dead livestock and damaged reputations could combine until a neighbour was treated as the cause of misfortune.

pages.title: When Belief Became Danger in Angola
pages.summary: Angola’s history of collective fear and contested belief is not dominated by a single famous “mass hysteria” episode. Its clearest cases instead involve children accused of witchcraft, prophetic Christian movements treated as political threats, and the deadly confrontation between police and followers of José Julino Kalupeteka at Mount Sumi in 2015.

pages.title: Child Accusations
pages.summary: Children accused of witchcraft were often blamed for hardship, rejected by relatives and subjected to abuse disguised as spiritual deliverance.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief Became Danger in Angola.

pages.title: Mount Sumi
pages.summary: The Mount Sumi confrontation became a disputed national tragedy in which religious suspicion, police force and conflicting death accounts collided.

pages.title: Tokoism
pages.summary: Simão Toko's movement became politically threatening to colonial authorities because an African-led church could organise outside missionary control.

pages.title: When Resistance, Ritual and Colonial Fear Collided
pages.summary: Antigua and Barbuda does not have a well-documented history of dance plagues, mass fainting outbreaks, UFO religions or modern destructive sects.

pages.title: 1736 Plot
pages.summary: The 1736 trials may have exposed a real resistance network, but coercion and planter panic probably enlarged the official story.

pages.title: Obeah Laws
pages.summary: Obeah laws turned diverse spiritual practices into a criminal category shaped by colonial ideas about fraud, danger and social control.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Antigua and Barbuda.

pages.title: Spiritual Power
pages.summary: African-derived oaths, divination and healing could strengthen solidarity while appearing dangerously secretive to slaveholders.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Public Force in Argentina
pages.summary: Argentina’s history of contagious belief is not dominated by one great witch craze or a single notorious apocalyptic sect.

pages.title: Sect Scare
pages.summary: Media reports turned diverse spiritual groups into a single public threat, often blurring eccentric belief, coercion and proven crime.

pages.title: Uritorco UFOs
pages.summary: Stories of lights, contactees and the hidden city of Erks turned Cerro Uritorco into a lasting centre of UFO spirituality and tourism.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Argentina.

pages.title: San Nicolas
pages.summary: A housewife's reported visions became a major pilgrimage movement after clergy supervised the messages and authorised public devotion.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Threat to Armenia
pages.summary: Armenia’s history of collective fear is not dominated by a single famous “mass hysteria” episode. Its strongest documented pattern is different: religious difference repeatedly became entangled with fears about national survival, foreign influence and political disloyalty.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief Became a Threat to Armenia.

pages.title: Medieval Heresy
pages.summary: Medieval religious dissent became a political threat when hostile labels blurred heresy, rebellion and territorial disloyalty.

pages.title: Sect Scare
pages.summary: After independence, missionaries and minority churches were often portrayed as foreign sects threatening families, military duty and national identity.

pages.title: Soviet Atheism
pages.summary: Soviet authorities used confiscation, propaganda and repression to recast organised religion as backward and politically dangerous.

pages.title: When Fear and Belief Gripped Australia
pages.summary: Australia has not experienced the large-scale witch trials or possession epidemics associated with early modern Europe, but it has produced its own distinctive history of contagious fears, disputed beliefs and high-control religious movements.

pages.title: Chamberlain Case
pages.summary: Lindy Chamberlain's wrongful conviction shows how religious prejudice, media suspicion and flawed expertise can turn rumour into legal certainty.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Belief Gripped Australia.

pages.title: Scientology
pages.summary: Australia's fight with Scientology raised a lasting question: when should governments regulate harmful conduct without outlawing belief?

pages.title: The Family
pages.summary: The Family shows why unusual beliefs are not the main issue when secrecy, isolation, coercion and violence shape daily life.

pages.title: When Fear Became Persecution in Austria
pages.summary: Austria’s history of collective fear is not a single story of irrational crowds. It is a series of episodes in which supernatural beliefs, rumours, political interests and genuine abuse became entangled.

pages.title: Witch Trials
pages.summary: The failed Innsbruck prosecution and Maria Pauer's execution reveal both resistance to witch hunting and its late survival.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear Became Persecution in Austria.

pages.title: Salzburg Hunt
pages.summary: Salzburg's hunt for the Sorcerer Jackl grew through torture, denunciation and hostility towards mobile poor communities.

pages.title: Vienna Gesera
pages.summary: The destruction of medieval Vienna's Jewish community shows how unsupported ritual accusations became organised state violence.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Public Threat
pages.summary: Azerbaijan has no well-established equivalent of the Salem witch trials, the European dancing plagues or a famous nationwide outbreak of mass psychogenic illness.

pages.title: Healing Shrines
pages.summary: Azerbaijan's healing shrines show how stories of protection and cure can spread without becoming a sudden mass panic.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Azerbaijan.

pages.title: Minority Faiths
pages.summary: Minority churches and Jehovah's Witnesses faced raids, fines and hostile labels as the state defined acceptable religion.

pages.title: Soviet Campaigns
pages.summary: Soviet authorities recast faith, pilgrimage and ritual as backward threats that had to be controlled or erased.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Public Crisis in Bahrain
pages.summary: Bahrain has no well-documented history of classic European-style witch trials, dance plagues or large outbreaks of mass psychogenic illness.

pages.title: Al Tajdeed
pages.summary: The campaign against Al Tajdeed shows how calling a religious group a cult can shape public fear, legal pressure and authority.

pages.title: Witchcraft Scares
pages.summary: Discoveries of buried writings and alleged talismans show how uncertain evidence can become a public scare demanding official action.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Bahrain.

pages.title: Qarmatians
pages.summary: The Qarmatians turned apocalyptic expectation into state power, warfare and a disastrous attempt to recognise a promised redeemer.

pages.title: When Fear Spread Across Bangladesh
pages.summary: Bangladesh’s clearest history of contagious fear is not a story of one famous “cult” or a single nationwide delusion. It is a series of sharply documented episodes in which bodily symptoms, religious accusations, kidnapping rumours and scarcity scares spread through schools, neighbourhoods and social media.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear Spread Across Bangladesh.

pages.title: Online Rumours
pages.summary: False or manipulated online accusations repeatedly helped mobilise crowds against vulnerable religious minorities.

pages.title: Bridge Rumour
pages.summary: A construction legend about human sacrifice fuelled child-abduction fears and deadly mob attacks in 2019.

pages.title: School Illness
pages.summary: Bangladesh's school outbreaks show how genuine symptoms can spread through fear, observation and shared expectations.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Threat in Barbados
pages.summary: Barbados does not have a well-documented history of classic “mass hysteria” episodes such as dancing plagues, contagious fainting outbreaks or large satanic-abuse scares.

pages.title: Quaker Scare
pages.summary: An alleged slave conspiracy turned Quaker meetings and Christian conversion into suspected routes to rebellion.

pages.title: 1816 Revolt
pages.summary: After the 1816 revolt, officials treated rituals, oaths and protective medicines as part of a wider machinery of rebellion.

pages.title: Obeah Laws
pages.summary: Colonial officials grouped healing, divination and spirit work under one criminal label that made diverse practices easier to police.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief Became a Threat in Barbados.

pages.title: Who Decided What Belarus Should Fear?
pages.summary: Belarus does not have a single famous episode equivalent to the Salem witch trials or the dancing plague of Strasbourg. Its history of contagious belief is more fragmented and, in some ways, more revealing.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Who Decided What Belarus Should Fear?.

pages.title: Sect Panic
pages.summary: Real crimes by a few movements helped turn the word sect into a sweeping label for many peaceful and unfamiliar religions.

pages.title: Soviet Atheism
pages.summary: Soviet authorities recast religion as ignorance and political danger, shifting collective suspicion from witches to committed believers.

pages.title: Witch Trials
pages.summary: Scattered trials show how illness, bad luck and damaged reputations could turn neighbourhood suspicion into legal persecution.

pages.title: When Fear and Faith Swept Through Belgium
pages.summary: Belgium’s history of collective fear and contagious belief is not one single story of “mass hysteria”. It ranges from lethal witch prosecutions in the early modern Southern Netherlands to twentieth-century Marian apparitions, anxiety about unconventional religions, and the extraordinary Coca-Cola health scare of 1999.

pages.title: Antoinism
pages.summary: Antoinism shows why the word cult can mislead when a healing religion is peaceful, decentralised and socially accepted.

pages.title: Apparitions
pages.summary: Children's visions, pilgrimage crowds and church investigations turned two Belgian villages into enduring centres of Marian devotion.

pages.title: Witch Trials
pages.summary: Belgium's witch panics became deadly when courts, torture and local reputations turned suspicion into legal proof.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Faith Swept Through Belgium.

pages.title: When Belief Became Fear in Belize
pages.summary: Belize does not have a well-documented national equivalent of the Salem witch trials, a medieval dancing plague or a large school outbreak of mass psychogenic illness. Its history of contagious belief and collective fear is quieter and more fragmented.

pages.title: Fear Folklore
pages.summary: Belize's supernatural beings shaped warnings about night travel, drinking and disobedience without producing a documented national panic.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief Became Fear in Belize.

pages.title: 2012 Scare
pages.summary: The supposed Maya doomsday prophecy was a global media invention that distorted ancient calendars and sidelined living Maya voices.

pages.title: Obeah Laws
pages.summary: Colonial law blurred the line between preventing fraud and punishing African-derived spiritual beliefs in British Honduras.

pages.title: When Fear, Faith and Power Collided in Benin
pages.summary: Benin’s history of collective fear is not dominated by one famous “mass hysteria” episode. Its most important cases are better understood as recurring struggles over witchcraft, dangerous births, epidemic disease and religious authority.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear, Faith and Power Collided in Benin.

pages.title: State Panic
pages.summary: Benin's revolutionary government turned fears of occult enemies into an official struggle over modernity, loyalty and religious authority.

pages.title: Sakpata
pages.summary: Smallpox gave Sakpata priests authority to diagnose danger, direct treatment and shape how communities understood sudden death.

pages.title: Tron
pages.summary: Travelling anti-witchcraft shrines promised protection but could also turn quarrels, illness and bad luck into evidence of hidden attack.

pages.title: How Fear and Rumour Spread in Bhutan
pages.summary: Bhutan does not have a well-documented history of classic witch trials, organised “cult” violence or large outbreaks of mass psychogenic illness comparable with better-known cases elsewhere.

pages.title: Pandemic Rumours
pages.summary: Pandemic rumours about infection, quarantine and vaccination forced Bhutanese authorities to pair health measures with constant reassurance.

pages.title: Rumour Networks
pages.summary: Trusted personal networks and fast-moving social media can make unsupported claims feel urgent before verification arrives.

pages.title: Headhunter Scare
pages.summary: In 2018, an unsupported headhunter story emptied streets and closed shops across parts of eastern Bhutan.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on How Fear and Rumour Spread in Bhutan.

pages.title: When Fear and Belief Took Hold in Bolivia
pages.summary: Bolivia’s history does not contain one famous, neatly bounded episode of “mass hysteria”.

pages.title: Colonial Idolatry
pages.summary: Spanish authorities turned local worship into evidence of idolatry, disloyalty and demonic influence.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Belief Took Hold in Bolivia.

pages.title: Kharisiri
pages.summary: Stories of fat-stealing strangers turn inequality, illness and intrusive outsiders into a vivid and sometimes dangerous threat.

pages.title: Ghost Rapes
pages.summary: Supernatural explanations concealed a sustained campaign of drugging and sexual assault against women and girls.

pages.title: When Belief Becomes Socially Powerful in Bosnia
pages.summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina does not have one famous, neatly bounded “mass hysteria” episode comparable with the Salem witch trials or a classic school fainting outbreak.

pages.title: Bosnian Pyramids
pages.summary: Visoko shows how tourism, national pride and scientific-sounding claims can keep a rejected archaeological theory alive.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Bosnia and Herzegovina.

pages.title: Medjugorje
pages.summary: Medjugorje became a global pilgrimage centre even though the Catholic Church has never declared its reported visions supernatural.

pages.title: Wartime Fear
pages.summary: During the Bosnian War, real violence and organised propaganda combined to turn fear, rumour and collective blame into weapons.

pages.title: When Fear Gripped Botswana's Schools and Streets
pages.summary: Botswana’s history of collective fear is not dominated by one notorious sect or a single nationwide “witch craze”. Its clearest documented episodes fall into two overlapping patterns: public alarm over alleged ritual murder and outbreaks of unexplained illness among schoolchildren.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear Gripped Botswana's Schools and....

pages.title: School Illness
pages.summary: Botswana's school outbreaks show how genuine symptoms can spread through stress and social contact without infection or poisoning.

pages.title: Segametsi Case
pages.summary: A schoolgirl's unsolved murder became a national crisis over ritual killing, elite protection and the state's use of force.

pages.title: Witchcraft Law
pages.summary: Botswana's witchcraft law tries to curb fraud and harm, yet its language may also preserve the fears it was meant to control.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Public Threat
pages.summary: Brazil’s history of collective belief and fear is not one story of “mass hysteria”.

pages.title: Canudos
pages.summary: Canudos became a national crisis when religious autonomy, republican insecurity and rumours of monarchist conspiracy reinforced one another.

pages.title: Contestado
pages.summary: The Contestado movement joined sacred prophecy to anger over dispossession, railway expansion and the failure of state protection.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Brazil.

pages.title: Padre Cicero
pages.summary: Padre Cicero's disputed miracle transformed Juazeiro into a pilgrimage centre and raised lasting questions about who may declare an event sacred.

pages.title: How Fear and Belief Spread in Brunei
pages.summary: Brunei’s best-documented episode of contagious fear is not a violent cult or historic witch trial, but a series of school outbreaks in which pupils screamed, shook, fainted, cried or said they were being disturbed by spirits.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on How Fear and Belief Spread in Brunei.

pages.title: How It Spread
pages.summary: Mass psychogenic illness explains how genuine symptoms can travel through fear, expectation and social contact without conscious imitation.

pages.title: State and Belief
pages.summary: Brunei's authorities answered spiritual scares through approved healing while restricting teachings officially labelled deviant.

pages.title: School Outbreaks
pages.summary: During exam season, fear and possession beliefs spread through several schools, affecting pupils and some adults.

pages.title: Who Defined Truth and Danger in Bulgaria?
pages.summary: Bulgaria’s history of contagious belief is not dominated by one famous outbreak of “mass hysteria”. Instead, it reveals a recurring struggle over who may define religious truth, credible knowledge and social danger. Medieval rulers and clergy portrayed the Bogomils as a subversive heresy.

pages.title: Bogomils
pages.summary: Bogomilism became dangerous to rulers because disputes over ritual and church wealth were recast as threats to public order.

pages.title: White Brotherhood
pages.summary: Peter Deunov's White Brotherhood joined Christian mysticism, disciplined communal practice and a national vision of spiritual transformation.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Who Defined Truth and Danger in Bulgaria?.

pages.title: Vampire Graves
pages.summary: Unusual Bulgarian burials reveal real fears of dangerous dead, but modern vampire stories often claim more than archaeology can prove.

pages.title: When Fear Turns Neighbours Into Suspects
pages.summary: Burkina Faso’s clearest documented history of contagious belief and collective fear is not a single spectacular outbreak of “mass hysteria”. It is the repeated accusation and expulsion of people—especially older women—said to have caused illness or death through witchcraft.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Burkina Faso.

pages.title: In Burkina Faso, Older Women
pages.summary: Gender inequality, bereavement, family conflict and property disputes often shape who is blamed and who can safely resist.

pages.title: After Banishment
pages.summary: Refuge centres can prevent immediate violence, but lasting safety depends on mediation, livelihoods and acceptance back home.

pages.title: Soul Eating
pages.summary: Unexpected deaths can trigger rumours, divination and self-reinforcing claims that an unseen attacker has consumed a victim's vital force.

pages.title: When Collective Belief Turns Dangerous in Burundi
pages.summary: Burundi’s best-documented history of contagious belief and collective fear is not a catalogue of classic “mass hysteria” outbreaks.

pages.title: Albinism Attacks
pages.summary: People with albinism were targeted when supernatural myths combined with poverty, criminal demand and weak protection.

pages.title: Businde
pages.summary: The Businde crisis grew from a disputed Marian movement, rival claims to religious authority and a lethal state response.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Burundi.

pages.title: Witchcraft
pages.summary: Witchcraft claims in Burundi have turned fear and misfortune into permission to attack vulnerable people.

pages.title: Why Collective Fear Took Hold in Cambodia
pages.summary: Cambodia’s history of collective fear and contagious belief is not best understood as a catalogue of bizarre “cults”. Its strongest documented cases sit at the meeting point of political upheaval, economic pressure, spiritual belief and unreliable information.

pages.title: Factory Faintings
pages.summary: Cambodia's garment-factory faintings emerged from a mix of physical strain, fear, workplace pressure and culturally familiar spirit beliefs.

pages.title: Holy Men
pages.summary: Cambodia's holy man rebellions joined political resistance to beliefs in sacred authority, moral renewal and supernatural protection.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Why Collective Fear Took Hold in Cambodia.

pages.title: School Scares
pages.summary: School outbreaks show how illness, stress, ghost rumours and visible fear can spread rapidly through groups of pupils.

pages.title: Why Hidden Enemies Became So Powerful in Cameroon
pages.summary: Cameroon’s history of collective fear is not dominated by one famous outbreak of “mass hysteria”. Its strongest documented pattern is different: recurring scares about witchcraft, secret wealth, hidden societies, spiritual attack and moral corruption.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Cameroon.

pages.title: Nyongo
pages.summary: Nyongo stories turned sudden prosperity into suspicion that relatives had been sacrificed or forced into invisible labour.

pages.title: Occult Panics
pages.summary: Rumours of hidden power grew strongest when inequality, migration and political distrust made ordinary success or misfortune hard to explain.

pages.title: Witchcraft Law
pages.summary: Cameroonian courts tried to contain witchcraft accusations, but criminal trials often gave supernatural claims official authority.

pages.title: When Fear and Faith Gripped Canada
pages.summary: Canada’s history of cults, collective scares and contagious belief is not one continuous story of irrationality.

pages.title: Doomsday Groups
pages.summary: The Ant Hill Kids and Solar Temple show how prophecy, dependency and isolation could escalate into documented abuse and death.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Faith Gripped Canada.

pages.title: Witchcraft
pages.summary: New France saw supernatural accusations and court cases, but never developed a Canadian equivalent of the Salem witch panic.

pages.title: Panic or Illness
pages.summary: Rumour-driven accusations and stress-related symptom outbreaks may spread socially, but they require very different evidence and responses.

pages.title: Where Fear, Faith and Colonial Power Collided
pages.summary: Cape Verde does not have a well-documented history of spectacular witch trials, dancing plagues or nationwide outbreaks of mass psychogenic illness.

pages.title: Charms and Healing
pages.summary: Christian prayers, protective objects and African-derived practices could be understood as healing by users and superstition by clergy.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Cape Verde.

pages.title: Rabelados
pages.summary: The Rabelados defended older Catholic practices but were cast as backward rebels under Portuguese colonial rule.

pages.title: Myth or Record
pages.summary: The surviving record supports scattered supernatural beliefs, but not a Cape Verdean Salem or documented mass psychogenic epidemic.

pages.title: Why Witchcraft Accusations Became So Dangerous
pages.summary: The best-documented history of contagious fear and collective belief in the Central African Republic is not a single spectacular “mass hysteria” event.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Central African Republic.

pages.title: Making Accusations
pages.summary: Illness, death and family conflict can become personalised accusations when communities seek an intentional cause for suffering.

pages.title: Wartime Hunts
pages.summary: Civil war made witchcraft accusations more lethal as armed groups used fear to punish enemies, extort communities and impose control.

pages.title: Witchcraft Law
pages.summary: Criminalising alleged witchcraft gives official force to unprovable claims and places older women at exceptional risk of imprisonment.

pages.title: When Fear and Power Shaped Belief in Chad
pages.summary: Chad does not have a well-documented national history of dance plagues, school fainting epidemics or apocalyptic sects comparable with the best-known cases elsewhere.

pages.title: Missing Record
pages.summary: Chad's surviving record points to persecution and coercive belief rather than classic outbreaks of contagious unexplained illness.

pages.title: Dosseye Panic
pages.summary: A cluster of deaths in Dosseye camp led to attacks on accused women and dangerous avoidance of medical care.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Power Shaped Belief in Chad.

pages.title: Political Sorcery
pages.summary: President Francois Tombalbaye used sorcery accusations and compulsory initiation to turn political loyalty into ritual obedience.

pages.title: When Belief, Fear and Power Shaped Chile
pages.summary: Chile’s history of collective belief and fear is not a single story of “mass hysteria”.

pages.title: Chiloe Witches
pages.summary: The 1880 Chiloe prosecution reveals how sorcery fears, local authority and state expansion became entangled.

pages.title: Colonia Dignidad
pages.summary: Colonia Dignidad shows how isolation, coercive leadership and official protection allowed documented abuse to continue for decades.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief, Fear and Power Shaped Chile.

pages.title: Penablanca
pages.summary: The Penablanca visions became a media phenomenon where faith, dictatorship-era anxiety and political suspicion converged.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Public Crisis in China
pages.summary: China’s history of collective fear and contagious belief is not a simple procession of “cults” and irrational crowds. It is a history of rumours meeting insecurity, religious hopes becoming political programmes, and governments treating unregulated belief as a possible threat to public order.

pages.title: Dangerous Belief
pages.summary: From White Lotus accusations to modern anti-cult campaigns, official labels have often blurred fraud, dissent, unregulated religion and rebellion.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief Became a Public Crisis in China.

pages.title: Sacred Rebellions
pages.summary: Promises of divine protection and a purified new order became engines of war when they met poverty, foreign intrusion and failing authority.

pages.title: Soul Stealers
pages.summary: Rumours of stolen souls became a national witch hunt as frightened communities, forced confessions and imperial suspicion reinforced one another.

pages.title: When Fear and Belief Swept Through Colombia
pages.summary: Colombia’s history of collective fear and contagious belief is not a simple catalogue of bizarre episodes. Its most revealing cases show how supernatural ideas, medical uncertainty, racial hierarchy, political violence and distrust of institutions can reinforce one another.

pages.title: Vaccine Illness
pages.summary: A wave of genuine symptoms among vaccinated schoolgirls became a national crisis after fear, media coverage and institutional distrust amplified it.

pages.title: Witch Trials
pages.summary: Cartagena's witchcraft prosecutions turned African healing traditions and social prejudice into an official system of punishment.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Belief Swept Through Colombia.

pages.title: Stella Maris
pages.summary: The disappearance of Stella Maris followers into the mountains became a national alarm despite limited evidence of planned mass harm.

pages.title: When Fear and Belief Shaped Comoros
pages.summary: Comoros does not have a well-documented national equivalent of the Salem witch trials, a famous “cult” disaster or a recognised epidemic of mass psychogenic illness.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear and Belief Shaped Comoros.

pages.title: Karthala
pages.summary: The 2005 Karthala evacuations show how real danger, weak information and frightening rumours can combine during a disaster.

pages.title: Possession
pages.summary: In Mayotte, possession was a recognised social and healing practice rather than a sudden epidemic of irrational behaviour.

pages.title: Religious Policy
pages.summary: Official fears of division and radicalisation helped turn religious difference into a matter of state control and public suspicion.

pages.title: When Belief Became a Threat in Congo
pages.summary: “Congo” does not have one neat history of mass hysteria or cults. The name covers two modern states — the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the smaller Republic of the Congo — as well as several colonial territories whose borders, rulers and official names changed repeatedly.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Belief Became a Threat in Congo.

pages.title: Kimbangu
pages.summary: Kimbangu's peaceful healing movement became a colonial security scare and later a powerful symbol of African religious independence.

pages.title: Child Witches
pages.summary: Children were blamed for illness and hardship as war, poverty, family breakdown and paid deliverance ministries intensified witchcraft fears.

pages.title: Kitawala
pages.summary: Colonial officials treated diverse Kitawala communities as one secret rebellion, turning suspicion and repression into apparent proof of conspiracy.

pages.title: When Fear Tested Costa Rica's Peaceful Image
pages.summary: Costa Rica has no well-documented equivalent of the Salem witch trials, a fatal millenarian commune or a nationwide outbreak of mass psychogenic illness. Its most revealing episodes are subtler: religious controversies, press-driven scares and moments when unfamiliar people were treated as threats to the country’s moral order.

pages.title: Hippie Scare
pages.summary: About ten visiting hippies became symbols of drugs, sexual freedom and foreign disorder far beyond any danger they posed.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on When Fear Tested Costa Rica's Peaceful Image.
